text: Simon Åke Strandvik and Anna Sophie Schedin now own the property at Valinge Rygg 24 in Varberg. The sellers are Anneli Maria Josarp, Jan Eric Sawarell, Greta Gunilla Lundqvist, Leif Anders Nilsson, Kjell Yngve Nilsson, Monica Birgitta Elisabeth Nilsson, Mari Helena Nilsson, Lise-Lotte Gabriella Nilsson, Karl Jörgen Nilsson, Ihrene Elisabeth Marguerite Aspling, Ann-Louise Ljungquist, Anna Maria Nilsson, and Lars-Göran Nilsson.

The charming residential building was erected in 1909 and is located in a scenic and secluded setting at the end of the road in Valinge. The property has a rich history and over the decades has served as a home for several generations of local families, but over time it has also housed newer operations. Today, the property – historically designated Rygg 3:7, now Rygg 24 – comprises the main house and three barns. It is a vibrant place offering overnight accommodation as well as space for courses, events, and celebrations.

The farm is not only a place for relaxation and smaller gatherings, but also serves as the stage for the intimate, private music festival FestiValinge. The festival was held, among other times, in August 2026, featuring live bands, DJs, and an open stage in the garden and barn.

In recent times, visitors and friends who have stayed overnight or looked after the farm have recounted strange and unusual occurrences on the property. Several people have both heard and seen phenomena suggesting a continued presence on the farm. Among other things, people have noticed a man who seems to walk around, puttering and keeping things in order in the house – closing doors that were left open, and clattering sounds are heard from the kitchen as if someone is standing there washing dishes. The experiences have primarily occurred when the owners were away and others were house-sitting, as if the man is also there to look after the property and keep a watchful eye over Lunden.

Sometime during the 1960s, the property was taken over by a Danish man (and his wife/partner). In connection with the change of ownership, an extensive full renovation was carried out, and during their time on the farm they ran, among other things, a dog boarding kennel. After this period, the house later came to stand empty, which unfortunately led to its decay – before the current owners took over, put in solid work, and brought Lunden back to life.

Arthur William Sixten Nilsson was born on March 23, 1910, in Abild and moved into the house on November 8, 1943. He worked as a control assistant, and the household also included his wife Junis Linnéa (née Gustavsson), born on June 4, 1914, in Varberg. They married on November 20, 1937, and had three daughters: Siv Elsa Anita (born February 25, 1938), Gerd Harriet Irène (born December 19, 1940), and Gudrun Elsie Margaretha (born November 29, 1945). The family also included a son, Gösta, who was born in the 1950s and therefore does not appear in the older parish records. Arthur passed away on June 13, 1986, and Junis on February 1, 1998; the couple rests together at St. Jörgen's Cemetery.

During Arthur's time, the property was expanded significantly. On April 3, 1945, the Nilssons bought a parcel of land of nearly 0.75 hectares (the so-called marsh parcel) from the neighboring property Rygg 6:1 for 1,400 SEK. The area was partitioned off and officially merged with Lunden (Rygg 3:7) in June 1946, growing the property to just over 1 hectare – a land purchase made so that they could feed a cow on the farm.

Before Arthur and his family took over, the house was owned and inhabited by the carpenter Johan Andersson, born on June 1, 1898, in Valinge. He was married to Anna Hildegard (née Johansson), born on July 15, 1902, in Valinge. The couple married on February 10, 1922, and it was in connection with the wedding that they took over the property. They had two daughters: Astrid Junia (born March 4, 1922, died March 12, 1997) and Inga-Marianne (born December 6, 1935). On October 20, 1944, the entire family moved out to settle in Lindberg. Johan passed away in 1968 and Anna on February 28, 1993. Johan is buried in Valinge alongside his wife and their eldest daughter Astrid.

Before Johan took over, the house was owned by his father, Sven Edvard Andersson, born on February 9, 1858, in Valinge and deceased on December 30, 1938. It was Sven who built the house on November 25, 1909. He lived there with his wife Hilma Maria Johansdotter, born on May 26, 1856, in Lindberg and deceased on July 4, 1926. They married on November 23, 1881, and had their son Johan. The household also included Augusta Josefina Andersdotter (born March 6, 1856, died June 10, 1918), who was likely a sister to Sven. Sven continued to live with Johan and his family until his death. Sven is buried in Valinge together with his wife and two other female relatives, possibly sisters.

The property Lunden has its historical origins in May 1905, when the landowner Nils Aron Carlsson sold a land area of 28 ares and 3 square meters (approx. 0.28 hectares) from the parent property 1/4 mantal Crown Tax Rygg No. 3 (Bengt Olsgård) for 1,000 SEK to the carpenter Johan Helander Karlsson. The land survey office in Halmstad confirmed the land parceling on August 12, 1905, under the property designation Rygg 3:7.

It was after this, around the year 1909, that the current residential house was built on the site by Sven Edvard Andersson, who later acquired the property before his son Johan Andersson took over upon his marriage in 1922.

Going even further back in time, we find Sven's father, Carl Petter Larsson (born August 6, 1830, in Valinge), who was a crofter at Rygg 4. Sven's mother was Johanna Andersdotter, born on December 28, 1818, in Valinge. In addition to Sven, the group of siblings included sister Matilda (born October 23, 1863) and brother Johan Anton (born June 22, 1856), who later moved to Rolfstorp in 1875. When Sven's mother Johanna passed away on April 16, 1883, the father Carl Petter remarried Britta Christina Bengtsdotter (born September 24, 1833) from Lindberg.

history.heading2: Historical Events and Legends in Valinge Parish
text: People have lived in the area for at least 3,000 to 4,000 years. The region is rich in remains from the Bronze Age and the Migration Period. The parish previously belonged to Himle hundred. The name Valinge was historically spelled Hvalinge. The Old Norse word 'hval' means ridge or wall, meaning the name refers to those who live by the ridge.

One of the biggest milestones in the parish's modern history occurred when the old medieval stone church in Valinge was demolished in 1886. In 1891–1892, the current church was completed in a proud Neo-Romanesque style. The construction was a major event for the entire district and required extensive efforts and transport from all the crofters and farmers in the parish. The church tower, however, was retained from a previous rebuild in 1840 and still bears King Karl XIV Johan's initials (CXJVJ) in ironwork on its facade.

During the 19th century, the Great Partitioning (Laga skifte) was carried out in Valinge parish, which fundamentally transformed the entire cultural landscape. Previously, houses were clustered tightly together in village centers, but with the reform, villages were broken up and families moved their residences and outbuildings directly out to their assigned land plots. It was this historical reform that laid the foundation for individual small homesteads – like Lunden at Rygg – to emerge and be partitioned off.

Everyday life in the countryside was also marked by hardships and disease. On March 20, 1814, four children died in the Varberg region during epidemics of whooping cough and measles – childhood diseases that claimed many young lives in Halland during this era. In Valinge, Lundby was among the affected areas when ten-month-old infant boy Johannes Börjesson died of whooping cough.

The parish's older history also contains dramatic individual court cases. In the local court records, an incident is documented from the days of the Great Northern War in 1711, when a baggage train driver in Valinge met a tragic death that was brought before the district court. It is one of the oldest individual criminal and tragic notices documented in the area's local history research.

During World War II, Valinge unexpectedly ended up at the center of events. On October 10, 1943, a large Allied bomber of the type Liberator Mk.III (belonging to the Royal Air Force) crashed in a field in the parish. The aircraft was returning home from a special mission when it ran out of fuel. The entire crew of seven Polish airmen managed to save themselves by parachuting north of Rolfstorp before the abandoned plane crashed.

In 1959, the area was shaken by the so-called Valinge Strike, when church caretaker Gustaf Nilsson went on strike. This led to a drawn-out and bitter trade union conflict that attracted significant attention. The strike became known for its dramatic aspects, where strikebreakers ('blacklegs') reportedly dug graves under the cover of night so that funerals could take place despite the blockade.

In Halland folklore, there are also traces of old legends about terrifying creatures, including Gloson – a dreaded ghost sow with glowing eyes and a saw-toothed back. According to belief, the sow appeared during dark winter nights and posed a particularly dangerous threat to anyone undertaking an 'årsgång' (a traditional divination walk).

One of the more classic folk legends from the area is recorded in the folklore archives. It is said that while a picture of the Devil was being painted in Valinge Church, the Devil himself appeared to the painters and hissed: 'No matter how hideous you paint me, I can make myself even more hideous!'
